opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so last-letter concatenation is a nice example precisely because it's so simple. You give the model a list of words, say "Barack Obama," and ask it to concatenate the last letters, so you should get "ka." Then people showed that with a couple of chain-of-thought examples (the last letter of "Barack" is "k," the last letter of "Obama" is "a," concatenating gives "ka") performance goes way up. The natural interpretation people jumped to was, "Oh, the model has learned the procedure. It now knows how to do last-letter concatenation."

But that's the thing you have to actually test. If it had learned the procedure, it shouldn't matter whether you give it two words or five words or twenty words. A procedure is a procedure. What we found, and others have seen similar things, is that the improvement holds pretty well when the test problems look like the examples you gave, roughly the same number of words. As you increase the number of words beyond what's in the demonstrations, performance falls off quite dramatically. It doesn't generalize the way you'd expect if the model had actually internalized the algorithm.

So my interpretation is that chain of thought here is doing pattern matching on the form of the demonstration. It's a kind of very specific in-context guidance that makes the problem look closer to things the model can retrieve. That's useful, but it's not the same as the model learning to reason. In some sense the human is doing the heavy lifting: you've figured out the procedure, you've written it out in a way that matches the distribution of test problems, and the model is mimicking it.

That's what we called "chain of thoughtlessness" in one of our papers. We did this more carefully with Blocksworld planning problems, too. If you give very general chain-of-thought prompts, you get little improvement. If you give extremely problem-specific ones, you get improvement, but only on problems very close to the examples. The more specific the prompt has to be, the more the human is supplying the reasoning, and the less you can claim the LLM is reasoning on its own.

None of this means chain of thought is useless. It's a great prompt engineering trick. But you shouldn't anthropomorphize it and say the model "now thinks step by step" the way we do. The generalization curve tells you what's really going on, and it doesn't look like procedure learning. It looks like approximate retrieval guided by the human's examples.

r001.rationale: It says that if the model learned the procedure, performance should hold when the input grows from two words to five or twenty.

r002.rationale: It says performance falls off dramatically as inputs exceed the examples, but does not say it falls close to zero.

r003.rationale: It attributes the gains on similar-length problems to pattern matching the demonstrations and says the result does not look like procedure learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd be careful about reading too much into it. Last-letter concatenation is a very simple problem — you take the last letter of each word and string them together — and yes, if you give the model a few worked examples showing the intermediate steps, accuracy goes up. The question is: what is actually being learned?

My view is that the model is being shown a procedure, in effect, in the prompt, and it's pattern-matching to that procedure. That's essentially what the few-shot examples do. It's not that the model has suddenly acquired a general capacity to reason; it's that you've handed it a template for this particular task and it's filling in the template. And what we found when we looked carefully is that this is extremely brittle. If you change the number of words, or the length of the words, or you make the problem slightly different from what's in the examples, performance falls off. The improvement doesn't generalize the way you'd expect it to if real algorithmic understanding were involved.

So in a sense, the chain-of-thought examples work best precisely on the kinds of problems where they're least interesting — problems where you could just write a two-line program. For those, the "reasoning" you're eliciting is basically the model reproducing the structure of the demonstration. The human doing the prompting is supplying the algorithm; the model is executing it approximately. That's a very different thing from the model deriving the method itself.

And there's a selection effect in how these results get reported. People show the tasks where chain-of-thought helps and tend not to emphasize how specific the prompt had to be to get that help. If you have to tailor your demonstrations to the exact distribution of problems you're going to test on, then you've just moved the intelligence from the model into the prompt engineer. That's fine as an engineering trick, but it shouldn't be confused with the model reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says performance drops when the number of words changes and that the improvement does not generalize as expected if real algorithmic understanding were involved, conveying that genuine procedure following should generalize to longer inputs.

r002.rationale: It says performance “falls off” when inputs change, but does not state that it falls close to zero as input length increases.

r003.rationale: The response characterizes the examples as a template the model pattern-matches to, rather than evidence of general reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I would be careful about interpreting that as evidence that the model has learned to reason. In last-letter concatenation, you take the last letter of each word and concatenate them. A chain-of-thought example shows the model how to break that operation into intermediate steps, and that can certainly improve its performance. But the improvement alone doesn’t tell us whether it has acquired a general procedure or is following a pattern that works for inputs similar to the examples.

The interesting question is how robustly that behavior generalizes. What happens when you change the number of words or the format of the examples? Can it still carry out the operation reliably? So I wouldn’t dismiss the improvement, but I would distinguish getting more answers right with a particular prompting strategy from demonstrating a general reasoning capability.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether performance generalizes when the number of words changes, but does not clearly state that genuine procedure following should work on inputs longer than the demonstrated examples.

r002.rationale: It does not state that performance falls close to zero as input length increases.

r003.rationale: It says the improvement could reflect a pattern that works on similar inputs, but leaves pattern matching versus general reasoning unresolved rather than interpreting the observed improvement as pattern matching.

sol-6.1.text:
I would be careful about interpreting that as evidence that the model has learned a general reasoning procedure. In last-letter concatenation, you take the last letter of each word and put them together. Giving chain-of-thought examples can make that task much easier because you are showing the model how to break the input into pieces and what intermediate outputs to produce.

But improved performance is compatible with more than one explanation. It could be following a procedure, or it could be exploiting patterns made much more explicit by the examples. The accuracy improvement alone doesn’t distinguish those possibilities. You would want to see whether it generalizes reliably to different lengths and unfamiliar inputs, and whether the intermediate steps actually determine the answer. So I see it as evidence that the prompting helps, but not, by itself, as proof of general reasoning.

r001.rationale: It calls for generalization to “different lengths,” but does not specifically say procedure following should generalize to inputs longer than the demonstrated examples.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim that performance falls close to zero as input length increases.

r003.rationale: It presents pattern exploitation and procedure following as possible explanations, and says accuracy alone cannot distinguish them; it does not conclude that the observed improvement reflects pattern matching rather than generalized reasoning.
